```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)

# draws a table; cells flagged in `ans` are drawn in the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && ans[[i]][[j]]
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

# chunk option tight_mar = TRUE trims the default plot margins
knitr::knit_hooks$set(tight_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before && isTRUE(options$tight_mar)) par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
})

y <- c(1, 1, 0, 1)
cover <- c(30, 20, 10, 30)
nll_const <- function(p, y) -sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
lik <- function(p) p^3 * (1 - p)
lik_cov_exact <- prod(dbinom(y, 1, plogis(-2.2 + 0.11 * cover)))
```

**NRES 746 -- Week 5, Lecture 2: Writing the Likelihood**

\ans{\textbf{Answer key} (not for student distribution). Answers are in magenta.}

**Hand this in Monday.** The instructor is not here today but make sure your
name is at the top and turn it in next Monday!

**Instructions:** Work alone on
Parts 1-3, check in with
your group, then work through Part 4 with your group.
Please keep laptops closed through Part 4 -- calculators/phones are fine
for arithmetic, and fractions are fine as final answers. You can use laptops and Rstudio for Part 5.
If you get stuck, note where and move on.

## Putting it in context

On Monday you went *forward*: you chose a data-generating model and
imagined the data it would produce. Today we go *backward*: the data are
already in hand (they are the "known", the fixed quantity),
and the question is what they tell us about the
parameters (which are the "unknown", or variable quantity).
The probability formulas are the ones you already know from Bolker Ch 4.

We will stay with the sage-grouse nest-fate example from Monday. Here are
four nests, with outcome $y_i=1$ if at least one egg hatched and
$y_i=0$ if the nest failed:

```{r nest-data}
nests <- data.frame(
  Nest = 1:4,
  Cover = c(30, 20, 10, 30),
  Outcome = c(1, 1, 0, 1)
)
knitr::kable(nests, col.names = c("Nest", "Sagebrush cover (%)",
                                  "Outcome (1 = hatched, 0 = failed)"),
             align = "ccc")
```

## Part 1: One observation (individual, ~4 min)

For now, suppose every nest has the same unknown
probability $p$ of success.

**1a.** Write down the probability of each possible outcome for a
single nest.

$P(y=1 \mid p) =$ \ans{$p$} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $P(y=0 \mid p) =$ \ans{$1-p$}

**1b.** Write a single formula that gives the probability of an observed
outcome $y$. Make sure the formula gives the correct answer for both possible outcomes of $y$ (0 or 1).

\ans{$P(y \mid p) = p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}$ \quad (also correct: $yp + (1-y)(1-p)$)}

> **Definition.** The **likelihood** of a parameter value is the
> probability of the data you actually observed, if that parameter
> value were the truth. It is written as a function of the parameter
> alone, with the data held fixed -- not as a conditional probability of
> the parameter given the data, even though it is built from one. A
> subscript marks how much data is held fixed behind the scenes: for a
> single observation, $\mathcal{L}_1(p) = P(y \mid p)$.

**1c.** Nest 1 hatched ($y_1=1$). Evaluate the likelihood of $p=0.75$
and of $p=0.25$ given this observation.

$\mathcal{L}_1(0.75) =$ \ans{0.75} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $\mathcal{L}_1(0.25) =$ \ans{0.25}

**1d.** In your formula from 1b, which symbol is the data and which is
the parameter?

\ans{$y$ is the data; $p$ is the parameter.}

## Part 2: Several observations (individual, ~8 min)

Now use all four nests. Assume every nest has the same success
probability $p$, and that the nests are independent of one another.

**2a.** Write the likelihood of all four observations, $\mathcal{L}_4(p)$,
in terms of your formula from 1b. We can assume all observations are independent!
Please use product notation ($\prod$) to write the likelihood.

\ansbegin

$$\mathcal{L}_4(p) = \prod_{i=1}^{4} p^{y_i}(1-p)^{1-y_i}$$

\ansend

**2b.** Plug in the observed outcomes and simplify to the form
$p^{j}(1-p)^{k}$. What are $j$ and $k$?

$j =$ \ans{3} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $k =$ \ans{1} \quad \ans{(so $\mathcal{L}_4(p) = p^3(1-p)$; $\binom{4}{3}p^3(1-p)$ also accepted)}

**2c.** Evaluate your answer to 2b at the three values of $p$ below.
Fractions are fine.

```{r fill-lik-table, fig.height=0.35+3*0.5, fig.width=4}
blank_table(
  headers = list("p", "Likelihood"),
  body = list(
    list("0.25", sprintf("3/256 = %.4f", lik(0.25))),
    list("0.50", sprintf("1/16 = %.4f", lik(0.5))),
    list("0.75", sprintf("27/256 = %.4f", lik(0.75)))
  ),
  col_widths = c(1, 1.6),
  cex = 0.95,
  ans = list(c(FALSE, TRUE), c(FALSE, TRUE), c(FALSE, TRUE))
)
```

**2d.** Add up your three likelihood values. Do they sum to 1? Should
they?

\ans{$46/256 \approx `r round(sum(lik(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))), 2)`$. No, and they shouldn't: a likelihood is not a probability distribution over $p$.}

**2e.** Plot your three values on the axes below, then sketch the whole
curve $\mathcal{L}_4(p)$ for $0 \le p \le 1$. Mark where you think the
peak is. Is that where you would have guessed from the raw data alone?

```{r sketch-axes, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.4}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 0.12), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "p", ylab = "Likelihood")
abline(v = seq(0, 1, 0.25), h = seq(0, 0.12, 0.03), col = "grey85")
curve(lik(x), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = ans_col)
points(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), lik(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)), pch = 16, col = ans_col)
abline(v = 0.75, lty = 2, col = ans_col)
box()
```

\ans{Peak at $p = 0.75$, matching 3 of 4 nests hatched.}

## Part 3: The log-likelihood (individual, ~3 min)

**3a.** Take the log of your product from 2a and use the log rules to
rewrite it as a sum. Write your result for a general set of $n$ nests
with outcomes $y_1, \ldots, y_n$.

$\ell_n(p) = \log \mathcal{L}_n(p) =$ \ans{$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i \log p + (1-y_i)\log(1-p)\right]$}

\ans{(equivalently $\left(\sum y_i\right)\log p + \left(n - \sum y_i\right)\log(1-p)$)}

**3b.** Suppose the monitoring program had 1,852 nests and each nest
contributed a likelihood of about 0.5. Roughly how big is the product
of all 1,852 terms? Note that standard computer arithmetic cannot store
positive numbers much smaller than $10^{-308}$. Why might you want to work
with the sum from 3a instead? What is its value here (feel free to use your phone or a calculator)?

\ans{$0.5^{1852} \approx 10^{`r round(1852 * log10(0.5))`}$, which a computer stores as 0 (underflow). The sum is an ordinary number: $1852 \log(0.5) \approx `r round(1852 * log(0.5), 1)`$.}

## Group check-in (~3 min)

Compare your answers to Parts 1-3 with your group. Where you differ,
argue it out and revise. Then answer together:

**Group question.** Multiplying the four nest likelihoods together
depended on an assumption. Name one biological reason it might fail for
real sage-grouse nests.

\ans{Independence. Any shared cause works, e.g. the same hen renesting, neighboring nests sharing predators, shared weather in a year.}

## Part 4: Adding the covariate (with your group, ~6 min)

Monday's model had success probability rising with sagebrush cover. A
logistic function keeps it between 0 and 1:

$$p_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + b x_i)}}$$

where $x_i$ is the cover around nest $i$. Every nest now has its own
$p_i$. Suppose a candidate pair of parameter values is $a=-2.2$ and
$b=0.11$. Here are the success probabilities it predicts (rounded) for
our four nests:

```{r pred-table}
nests$p_pred <- c(0.75, 0.50, 0.25, 0.75)
knitr::kable(nests, col.names = c("Nest", "Sagebrush cover (%)",
                                  "Outcome (1 = hatched, 0 = failed)",
                                  "Predicted p"),
             align = "cccc")
```

**4a.** Check the predicted $p$ for nest 2 (20% cover) by hand.

\ans{$-2.2 + 0.11(20) = 0$, so $p_2 = 1/(1 + e^{0}) = 0.5$.}

**4b.** Assuming the nests are independent, what is the likelihood of
this candidate parameter pair, $\mathcal{L}_4(a=-2.2, b=0.11)$?
Careful with the nest that failed.

\ans{$0.75 \times 0.5 \times (1 - 0.25) \times 0.75 = 27/128 \approx 0.211$ (unrounded $p_i$: `r round(lik_cov_exact, 3)`).}

**4c.** Compare this to the best of your three constant-$p$ likelihoods
from 2c. Which model do the data support more, and by what factor? Does
that show that cover really matters for nest success? Give at least one
reason for caution.

\ans{Covariate model, by a factor of 2 ($27/128$ vs. $27/256$). No: e.g. only four nests; two parameters vs. one; $(a, b)$ wasn't fitted; no measure of uncertainty.}

**4d.** Write the likelihood for $n$ nests in general, $\mathcal{L}_n(a, b)$,
using $p_i = 1/(1+e^{-(a+bx_i)})$. Then underline the quantities that are
fixed data and circle the quantities that the likelihood is a function of.

\ansbegin

$$\mathcal{L}_n(a, b) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}, \qquad p_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + b x_i)}}$$

Underlined (data): $y_i$, $x_i$ (and $n$). Circled: $a$, $b$.

\ansend

## Part 5: From math to R code (with your group, ~10 min)

Later in the course you will fit models like this by writing the
likelihood as an R function and handing it to an optimizer. This is
your first try, so expect a little trial and error -- that's normal.

The built-in `dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = p)`
gives the Bernoulli probability from Part 1: `x` is the observed outcome
(0 or 1), `size` is the number of trials per observation, and `prob` is
the success probability. Setting `log = TRUE` returns the log of the
probability.

**5a.** Type this function into R, filling in the blanks so it returns
the *negative* log-likelihood of a vector of nest outcomes `y` for a
single success probability `p`. Run it -- if R complains, that's useful
information, not a failure.

\ansbegin

```{r nll-const-answer, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, highlight=FALSE}
nll_const <- function(p, y) {
  -sum(dbinom(x = y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
```

\ansend

**5b.** Run `y <- c(1, 1, 0, 1)`, then `exp(-nll_const(0.5, y))`. Which
entry of your table in 2c should it match? If it doesn't, use the
mismatch to track down the bug.

\ans{`r exp(-nll_const(0.5, y))`, the $p = 0.50$ row ($1/16$).}

**5c.** Run the code below with your own working `nll_const`.
(`sapply()` evaluates a function at each value of a vector in turn.)

```{r nll-grid-plot, echo=TRUE, tight_mar=TRUE, fig.width=4.5, fig.height=2.4}
p_grid <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.01)
nll_vals <- sapply(p_grid, function(p) nll_const(p, y))
plot(p_grid, nll_vals, type = "l", xlab = "p",
     ylab = "neg. log-likelihood", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 1, 0.25))
abline(v = seq(0, 1, 0.25), col = "grey85")
```

Which value of $p$ gives the smallest negative log-likelihood? Does it
agree with your sketch in 2e? Why do you think we work with the
*negative* log-likelihood rather than the log-likelihood?

\ans{$p = 0.75$; yes. Optimizers minimize by default (like SSR); minimizing $-\ell$ is the same as maximizing $\ell$.}

**Reflection.** (individual) Now that you've written and run your first
likelihood function, what part of turning the math into code gave you
the most trouble? And more generally, what is still fuzzy about
likelihood -- what would you like the instructor to review on Monday?

\ans{Open-ended.}

**5d. Optional challenge.** Write the covariate version, using your
formula from 4d.

\ansbegin

```{r nll-cover-answer, echo=TRUE, highlight=FALSE}
nll_cover <- function(par, y, cover) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(par[1] + par[2] * cover)))
  -sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
```

\ansend

If you ran `exp(-nll_cover(c(-2.2, 0.11), y, cover))`, what number
should you get, approximately, and why?

\ans{About `r round(exp(-nll_cover(c(-2.2, 0.11), y, cover)), 3)`: the likelihood from 4b (slightly different because 4b used rounded $p_i$).}
